index.html.text:
Supabase RLS Exposure Checker

Paste your Supabase project URL and anon key. This reads the project's own public schema listing to find every table the anon key can see, then sends one capped, read-only request per table and names which ones return real rows to an unauthenticated request — the missing-Row Level Security (RLS) exposure behind CVE-2025-48757 and the 170+ affected apps in 2025. Only run this against a project you own or are authorised to test.

Run the check

Enter your project URL and anon key, then click Check.

Report

Every table checked

TableResultDetail

Prefer a CLI for CI?

Same check, same modules, no browser:

node check.mjs https://abcdefghijklmno.supabase.co eyJhbGciOi... --json

Get check.mjs, probe.mjs, and analyze.mjs from the repo — exit code 1 if any table is exposed, so you can gate a deploy on it. Run it after every migration that adds a table: RLS off is the default for a brand-new table on projects created before Supabase changed that default in 2026, and it takes exactly one forgotten table to reopen this.

Common questions

Isn't the Supabase anon key supposed to be public?

Yes -- Supabase's own model treats the anon key as safe to embed in client-side code, and it appears in the JavaScript bundle of every app that uses the project. What is not supposed to be public is your actual table data. Row Level Security (RLS) is the only thing standing between that public key and your rows: the anon role's default schema USAGE grant already lets it see the schema, so a table with RLS off (or a policy broader than intended) is readable by anyone who has ever loaded your app and opened the network tab.

What actually happened in CVE-2025-48757?

A vulnerability class affecting apps built with AI app-builder platforms (Lovable was the most widely reported) where generated Supabase tables were left without RLS enabled. Security researchers found 170+ applications and 303+ endpoints where the public anon key could read, and in some cases write, every row in tables that were never meant to be public -- including, in at least one 2026 incident, admin emails and internal schema metadata. More background: why disabling RLS exposes your data.

Is it safe to paste my anon key into this page?

The anon key is designed to be public -- it is already in your app's client-side bundle. This page never sends it (or your project URL, or anything it reads back) to our servers: every request goes straight from your browser to your own project's REST endpoint, the same way your app's own client already talks to it. Still, only run this against a project you own or are authorised to test.

How is this different from Supabase's own dashboard Security Advisor?

The dashboard Advisor lints your database configuration and needs you to be logged in as a project member. This tool checks the live REST API from the outside using only the anon key, the same view an attacker, an external auditor, or a developer without dashboard access would have -- useful when you've inherited a project, are auditing someone else's app with permission, or want a check that needs no login at all. See the full comparison against checking RLS in the dashboard by hand, or how this compares to a third-party scanner service.

Does a clean report mean my project is secure?

No. This checks one specific, well-documented exposure -- can the anon key read real rows from a table -- using a capped, read-only request per table. It does not test authenticated roles, storage buckets, Edge Functions, write/update/delete access, or anything past what the anon key's schema listing reveals. Treat a clean report as evidence about this one exposure, not a full security audit.

Evidence, not a determination. This checks one specific, well-documented exposure using a capped, read-only request per table it can see in the project's own schema listing. It never writes, updates, or deletes anything, does not test authenticated roles, storage, or Edge Functions, and cannot see an exposure outside what the anon key's schema listing reveals. A clean report describes what this run found, not a guarantee the project has no exposure.

vs-manually-checking-the-dashboard.html.text:
← Supabase RLS exposure checker

This checker vs. checking RLS in the Supabase dashboard by hand

The Supabase dashboard already gives you two ways to look at RLS: Table Editor, which browses your table data, and the Advisor, which lints your project's configuration and flags a table with RLS switched off. Both are useful, and both answer a different question than the one this checker answers.

This checker sends one capped, read-only GET per table, using the anon key you provide, and reports which tables actually return real rows to that unauthenticated request -- the same request any visitor's browser (or curl) can already send. It does not read your policies, your RLS toggle state, or anything in the dashboard; it only reports what the anon key's own request actually got back.

Which one answers your question

What you are trying to find outWhere to look
Is there any table in this project with RLS switched off entirely? Either -- Advisor's lint catches this at a glance if you are logged in, and so does this checker.
Does a table with RLS enabled still return real rows to the anon key, because its policy is broader than intended? This checker. Advisor's lint is a binary off/on read of the RLS toggle -- it does not evaluate what an enabled policy's USING clause actually returns.
If I open Table Editor and see data, does that mean the anon key can read it too? No, and neither view answers this on its own. Table Editor runs as your own project session and shows you the data regardless of RLS. This checker sends the anon-key request itself and reports the real response.
Is a table returning zero rows because RLS is correctly blocking the anon key, or because the table is simply empty? This checker's unconfirmed category names that ambiguity explicitly rather than guessing. Neither dashboard view distinguishes the two either, since both show you the table's real, unfiltered state as its owner.
Can I run this without a dashboard login, project-member access, or a service-role key? This checker, and its CLI -- the anon key is the only credential it uses, the same one your own app's client already holds.
Can I gate a deploy on this in CI, unattended, without storing a dashboard session anywhere? This checker's CLI -- exit code 1 on any exposed table.

These are not a replacement for each other. Advisor is worth reading regularly as a configuration lint, and Table Editor is how you manage your own data day to day. This checker fills the gap between them: what the anon key's own request actually returns, checked the same way after every deploy rather than only when someone remembers to look.

Common questions

If I open Table Editor and see rows, doesn't that mean the anon key can read them?

No. Table Editor runs as your own logged-in project session, which is built to show you your data for management regardless of what RLS would do to an outside request -- that is the whole point of an admin data browser. Seeing rows there tells you the data exists; it tells you nothing about what an unauthenticated anon-key request actually receives. This checker sends that exact request -- the same one any visitor's browser can send -- and reports the real response.

Doesn't the Advisor already flag missing RLS?

It flags a table where RLS is switched off entirely, and it is a genuinely useful lint -- but that binary check does not evaluate what an enabled policy's USING clause actually returns. A table can have RLS turned on and still hand the anon role every row, if the policy attached to it is broader than intended (a common shape when a policy is copied from another table, or written as a quick USING (true) during development and never tightened). Advisor's lint reads as clean on that table; this checker does not read the policy at all -- it sends the request and reports what came back.

How do I know a table returning zero rows is actually safe, and not just empty?

Neither the dashboard's own views nor a policy read-through resolves this on their own -- an empty table and a table RLS is correctly blocking look identical from the anon key's side: zero rows, no error. This checker reports that case as its own category, unconfirmed, rather than guessing either way, and names the one way to resolve it: insert one throwaway test row and re-run, or check the row count from the dashboard directly as the table owner.

Do I need to be logged into the Supabase project either way?

Table Editor and Advisor both need a project member session -- they are dashboard features. This checker, and its CLI, need only what your own app's client already has: the project URL and the anon key. No account, no login, and the CLI's exit code 1 on any exposed table means it can gate a CI pipeline unattended without holding a dashboard session or a service-role key.

It is not a full security assessment and cannot see an exposure outside what the anon key's own schema listing reveals.

vs-vibeappscanner.html.text:
← Supabase RLS exposure checker

This checker vs. VibeAppScanner

VibeAppScanner is a hosted third-party service that scans Supabase and other AI-app-builder backends for security issues, including missing-RLS exposure, and returns a report. It is one of several services and write-ups that emerged from the same 2025-2026 wave of reporting on CVE-2025-48757 and the "170+ Lovable apps" incident this checker's own background page describes.

This checker does one narrower thing, differently. It reads your project's own PostgREST schema listing (an OpenAPI document the anon key can already see), then sends one capped, read-only GET per table it finds and reports which ones return real rows to that unauthenticated request. The code is open source and readable in full before you trust it, it runs entirely in your own browser tab (or as a Node CLI you can wire into CI), and it never sends your project URL, anon key, or anything it reads back to any server of ours.

Which one answers your question

What you are trying to doWhere to do it
Get a broader security report across more than RLS exposure, without reading any code yourself. VibeAppScanner or a comparable hosted scanning service.
Check specifically whether the anon key can read real rows from any table, with the smallest possible trust surface (nothing sent to a third party, code you can read line by line). This checker -- runs in your own browser, or as a CLI you control.
Gate a deploy in CI the moment a new table lands without RLS, unattended, on a runner where you would rather not hold a third-party API credential. This checker's CLI -- exit code 1 on any exposed table.
Audit a client's or a third party's project where you are only comfortable running something you can fully inspect first. This checker -- open source, no account, no hosted service seeing the key.
Want a managed dashboard, scheduled scanning, or support from a vendor. VibeAppScanner or a comparable paid/hosted service -- this checker is a free, unattended, no-account tool with no dashboard.

These are not mutually exclusive. A reasonable setup pairs a broader hosted scan run occasionally with this checker wired into CI as a tight, zero-trust-surface regression gate against the one exposure that has actually cost real incidents in 2025-2026: a newly created table with RLS left off.

Common questions

Should I use this checker or VibeAppScanner?

They serve overlapping but differently-shaped needs. VibeAppScanner is a hosted, broader security-scanning service covering more than RLS exposure across Supabase and other AI-app-builder backends, aimed at a developer who wants a fuller report without reading any code. This checker does one thing -- reads your project's own schema listing and tests whether the anon key can read real rows from each table -- with source code you (or anyone) can read in full before trusting it, runs entirely in your own browser with nothing sent to a third party, and has a CLI you can wire into your own CI. Reach for a hosted scanner when you want a broader audit and are comfortable with a third-party service seeing your project URL and key; reach for this when you want the narrower RLS-read check with the smallest possible trust surface.

Why would the trust surface matter if the anon key is public anyway?

The anon key is meant to be public, but that does not make every use of it equally low-risk to hand to a third party: a hosted scanner still becomes a service that has your project URL and key on its own servers, logs, and infrastructure, subject to its own security and retention practices. This tool never receives either -- every request goes directly from your browser to your project's own REST endpoint, the same way your app's client already talks to it, and nothing about the run is sent to us or stored anywhere but your browser's local storage as an anonymous usage count.

Is this page affiliated with VibeAppScanner?

No. This site is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by VibeAppScanner, and VibeAppScanner is a trademark of its owner, named here only to describe what this checker is and is not. The description of VibeAppScanner on this page is drawn from its own public site; check it there for what its current scan covers.

Only point either tool at a project you own or are authorised to test. That rule is unchanged by which one you pick.

why-does-disabling-rls-expose-my-supabas.text:
← Supabase RLS exposure checker

Why disabling RLS exposes your Supabase data

Supabase's REST API (PostgREST) is designed to be called directly from a browser tab -- that is the whole point of the anon key: it is meant to sit in your app's public JavaScript bundle, the same as a Firebase web config or a Stripe publishable key. What keeps that safe is not the key being secret. It is Row Level Security (RLS), a PostgreSQL feature that restricts which rows a query is allowed to touch, and Supabase's own model puts the entire enforcement burden on it: the anon role already has a schema-level USAGE grant the moment a table exists, so the only thing standing between the public key and every row in that table is whether RLS is turned on and a policy actually restricts it.

What happens when RLS is off

A table with RLS disabled behaves, over the REST API, as if any policy allowed everything: a plain unauthenticated GET to /rest/v1/<table> with only the anon key returns every row. Not a subset scoped to "your own" anything -- every row, to every visitor, including one who never logged in. The same is true for POST/PATCH/ DELETE if the anon role also has the corresponding grant, which is Supabase's default for a freshly created table.

This is not hypothetical -- CVE-2025-48757

In 2025, security researchers found this exact pattern across applications built with AI app-builder platforms, most widely reported for Lovable: generated Supabase tables were left without RLS enabled, and 170+ applications and 303+ endpoints turned out to be readable (and in some cases writable) by anyone with the project's public anon key -- which, again, is not a secret an attacker needs to steal, because it is already in the page source. A 2025 analysis of AI-generated apps found roughly one in ten tested applications exposed a vulnerable Supabase endpoint this way. Reporting into 2026 continued to find fresh instances, including at least one case where an AI platform's own database was exfiltrated after an attacker found a table with RLS missing and pulled admin emails and internal schema metadata out of it.

Why this stays easy to reintroduce

Supabase improved its defaults in 2026 -- new tables get RLS enabled by default in current projects, and the dashboard now flags and emails project owners about tables that lack it. That closes the gap for a brand-new project, not for one created before the change, and not for the ordinary case where RLS is enabled correctly on 30 tables and the 31st, added in a migration six months later, is not. The dashboard's own Security Advisor lint catches this too -- but only for someone logged in as a project member looking at it, which is exactly the moment a live check from the outside, using only the key any visitor's browser already has, earns its keep.

Check your own project

A free tool that runs exactly the check above -- reads your project's schema listing, requests one row from each table it finds, and names which ones return real rows to an unauthenticated request -- is at the Supabase RLS exposure checker. It runs entirely in your browser (or as a CLI for CI), and never sends your project URL, key, or anything it reads back to any server of ours. As with any tool that sends requests to a project you name, only run it against one you own or are authorised to test.
